DATE: March 17, 2025

Senator Rafferty, Representative Murphy and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education
and Cultural Affairs, I am Becky Smith, Director of Government and Community Relations for the
Maine Community College System and I am here today to testify neither for nor against LD 722 An Act
to Fund an Administrative Structure of an Emergency Medical Services Education Program in the Community College System. I would like to start by saying that I appreciate Representative Salisbury's
commitment to both Maine EMS and to the Maine Community College System. Our position of "Neither For Nor Against" is not because we believe that the funds dedicated to us for our EMS programs are not
needed---they are---it is only because, as you well know, we have discussed our priorities with this committee numerous times. Our priorities are an increase to our general operating budget along with ongoing funding for the Maine Free College program and funds that benefit our campuses and students
no matter their course of study.

Because your committee has not discussed our EMS program before, I would like to give you a bit of
information. The Maine Community College System has educated emergency responders for decades and trains a significant number of new responders annually. Our training centers have been critical partners to
the EMS system in Maine. In response to the increased need for emergency responders exacerbated by the COVID pandemic, in 2021 we created an EMS One Model led by the four colleges that offered EMS education programs in 2020, EMCC, KVCC, NMCC, and SMCC. The overarching goal of this project was to work collaboratively to stabilize the existing programs, to expand EMS education by adding new
programs at YCCC and WCCC and additional capacity at the other colleges; and to build a support
network across the state to ensure the ongoing viability of EMS education, especially in rural areas. This

collaboration standardized program structure and has enabled the colleges to align and share curriculum 9
develop a new curriculum for EMT and Advanced EMT, share instructors and provide joint instructor
training and update Training Center Standards, and implement Psychomotor portfolio testing across all
programs. The demand for EMS education statewide has never been higher, and this collaborative
approach has been critical in our efforts to help meet those demands, especially in rural areas, and provide equitable access across the state. Six of our colleges and our Harold Alfond Center for the
Advancement of Maine's Workforce now offer some level of EMS training. Our colleges support high
school programs at the CTEs to build a career pathway and engage potential responders early in their
education. We train hundreds of Mainers annually so they can become EMTs or increase their skills and become Advanced EMTs or Paramedics. We use funds from MJRP and the Harold Alfond Center to partner with private EMS providers, municipalities and others to train hundreds more without cost to the
student and either no cost or minimal cost to our municipalities.
The MCCS and the EMS programs at the colleges are committed to build from this foundation and further improve education and support the needs of the EMS system across the state. We are actively developing a plan to further stabilize and improve the delivery of EMS education statewide but that plan is still under development and a cost estimate yet to be determined. We appreciate Representative Salisbury's support for EMS education and the MCCS and hope that we can partner in the future to
implement this plan.

On behalf of the Maine County Commissioners Association, we appreciate the opportunity to provide testimony to this Committee in support of LD 722.
About MCCA. Briefly, the Maine County Commissioners Association was established in 1890 to assist Maine's county government in providing vital services to Maine citizens in a responsive, efficient, and credible manner. The Association is based in Augusta, represents all 16 of Maine's counties, and is governed by a board with representation from each participating county.
What does LD 722 do? LD 722 would appropriate $5,000,000 per year for FY 26 and FY 27 to establish and maintain an emergency services education administrative structure within Maine's community college system.
Discussion. Emergency medical services organizations and EMS personnel provide critical services to communities and work to ensure the health and safety of all people across our state. However, these organizations are struggling to maintain services, particularly in rural parts of the state. Two years ago, the Legislature established a commission to evaluate the challenges confronting EMS agencies in Maine, and county government was represented on that commission. One of the recommendations of the Commission was to establish an education program within Maine's community college system that will increase accessibility and potentially allow prospective students to remain close to home, especially in more rural areas of the state where the need for EMS personnel is greatest. We support this recommendation.

Good morning, Senator Rafferty, Representative Noonan Murphy, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on Education and Cultural Affairs, thank you for the opportunity
to present this bill before you today. I am Sue Salisbury, and I represent House District 128,
which includes part of Westbrook. I am here today to present LD 722, An Act to Fund an
Administrative Structure of an Emergency Medical Services Education Program in the
Community College System.
Since my first session in the House, I have been working with stakeholders to bring about change
in Maine Emergency Medical Services (EMS). Many of you have heard about the workforce
challenges and concerns related to funding and reimbursements from providers in your area. In
the 131$` Legislature, we provided a historic allocation of $31 million to Maine EMS. While the
distribution of funds has been slow, some progress is being made. Through rulemaking, Maine
EMS has recently recommended that $7.5 million go to Maine-EMS training centers and $1
million go to Regional Councils.
The goal of this bill is to help support this new direction that Maine EMS is taking by
permanently allocating $5 million per year from the general fund to the Community College
System. This would establish and maintain the EMS education administrative structure required by Maine EMS rules and extemal accreditation standards for EMS education.

Draft Proposed Structure:
$5 million for the Maine Community College system to develop and support an EMS program
